cards.text: Meet Micah the Moreshite. The word of the LORD comes to him in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. And what he sees is about two cities: Samaria and Jerusalem.
Micah doesn't ease into this one. No small talk, no 'how's everybody doing,' he just GRABS the mic.

cards.question: Micah opens with a call to listen. Who does he call to hear him?

answers.text: All peoples and the whole earth

cards.text: He says, "May the Lord GOD bear witness against you, the Lord from His holy temple." Because look: the LORD comes forth from His dwelling place to come down and tread on the high places of the earth.

cards.question: When the LORD treads on the high places of the earth, what do the mountains beneath Him do?
While the mountains melt beneath the LORD, the valleys hold firm.

cards.text: So what's all this shaking for? Micah says, "All this is for the transgression of Jacob and the sins of the house of Israel."

cards.question: Micah asks, "What is the transgression of Jacob?" Which city does he point to?
Then Micah asks about the high place of Judah, and the city he names is ___.

cards.text: Friend, Micah isn't pointing at some town way out on a back road. It's like the boss calls a meeting about who keeps taking cookies from the break room, and the crumbs lead STRAIGHT to the corner office.
Now the LORD speaks, and friend, it's HEAVY. He'll make Samaria a heap of rubble in the open field, a planting area for a vineyard, with her stones poured into the valley and her foundations exposed.

cards.question: Along with the city itself, the LORD says He will destroy all of Samaria's ___.

cards.text: Her carved images get smashed to pieces, and her wages go into the fire. The LORD says, "Since she collected the wages of a prostitute, they will be used again on a prostitute."

cards.question: After hearing what's coming for Samaria, Micah says he will lament and wail.

cards.text: Micah says he'll walk barefoot and naked, howl like a jackal and mourn like an ostrich. Friend, I took it hard when they slid me into that junk drawer, but I never went full OSTRICH.

cards.question: Micah says Samaria's wound is incurable. How far has it spread?

cards.text: Now Micah's lament goes town by town. It starts with this: "Do not tell it in Gath; do not weep at all."

cards.question: Micah is mourning what's coming. What does he tell the people of Beth-leaphrah to do?

cards.text: Shaphir departs in shameful nakedness. Zaanan won't come out, and Beth-ezel is in mourning.
The people of Maroth pined for good. But calamity came down, even to the gate of Jerusalem.

cards.question: The calamity that came down on Maroth came from the LORD.

cards.text: Next up, Lachish: "Harness your chariot horses, O dweller of Lachish." Friend, that's 'grab your keys, we're leaving RIGHT NOW.'

cards.question: Micah says the transgressions of Israel were found in Lachish. He calls Lachish the beginning of ___ to the Daughter of Zion.

cards.text: Then Micah says, "send farewell gifts to Moresheth-gath." That's the goodbye card the whole office signs.

cards.question: Micah says the houses of Achzib will prove dependable to the kings of Israel.
Then comes word for Mareshah. What is coming against Mareshah again?

cards.text: And the glory of Israel will come to Adullam. Then Micah's last call: shave yourselves bald, cut off your hair, "make yourselves as bald as an eagle."

cards.question: Why does Micah tell the people to shave themselves bald?

answers.text: To keep a vow to the LORD

cards.question: Micah says their precious children will go from them into ___.

cards.text: Their precious children, carried off into exile. Friend, I still miss my six little ones every day, so that line hits me right in the apron.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 8 quotes "send farewell gifts to Moresheth-gath.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 11 quotes "make yourselves as bald as an eagle.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: This story card is only a joke (no small talk, he grabs the mic). It tells nothing from Micah 1:2, but it still cites that verse. The joke has no passage moment to ride on.

rule.text: Every story card tells part of the passage. Jokes ride along on those cards.

findings.problem: The right answer stands out. Both wrong answers start with 'Only' and are narrow, while the right answer is longer and sweeping. A baker can pick it from the shape of the answers alone.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: 'So what's all this shaking for?' calls the events 'shaking'. Micah 1:4 says the mountains melt and the valleys split apart. The text never describes shaking.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: This story card is only a joke about the answers already given on cards 8 and 9 (Samaria and Jerusalem). It tells no new part of the passage, so it works as a recap.
'I never went full OSTRICH' makes Micah's sincere grief over the coming judgment the punchline. It implies that he overdid it, so the joke laughs at Micah's lament instead of with him.

rule.text: Humble. When a joke needs someone to laugh at, it's himself. Humor about people in Bible stories laughs with their human situation, never at them.

findings.problem: Micah 1:11 says 'Depart in shameful nakedness, O dwellers of Shaphir,' which is a command. The card narrates it as a fact: 'Shaphir departs in shameful nakedness.'

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: This one story card carries three separate moments: Shaphir, Zaanan and Beth-ezel.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: 'That's grab your keys, we're leaving RIGHT NOW' explains the command as a call to flee. Micah 1:13 doesn't say why Lachish should harness its chariot horses. It could be for flight or for battle, so the text leaves this open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The last story card restates the exile line that card 13 just asked about, then adds Papa Dorin's reaction. It tells no new part of the passage.

Micah 1:10-15 is a town-by-town lament (Gath, Beth-leaphrah, Shaphir, Zaanan, Beth-ezel, Maroth, Lachish, Moresheth-gath, Achzib, Mareshah, Adullam). The walkthrough gives it several choice cards on details about single towns. The docs list 'town lists' as a long stretch, and they say a stretch counts if it is 'mostly detail and not much happens'. But they also say speeches are not a long stretch, and this is part of a prophet's spoken message.
findings.question: Does a prophetic lament that moves through a list of towns, like Micah 1:10-15, count as a long stretch? If it does, it would get one summary story card and no choice cards. If it doesn't, it gets regular story and choice cards about each town.
